title: Paint Finishes Explained: Flat, Eggshell, Satin, Semi-Gloss
description: Use flat for ceilings, eggshell for living rooms, satin for kitchens and baths, and semi-gloss for trim. Here is how each sheen holds up.
seoTitle: Paint Finishes Explained: Flat, Eggshell, Satin, Semi-Gloss

cover.alt: Illustration of a paint fan deck on a painting blueprint background with a measuring tape

takeaways: Higher sheen means more shine, more washability, and more visible wall flaws, in that order every time.
Behr puts flat on low traffic walls and ceilings, eggshell in living rooms, satin in kitchens and baths, and semi-gloss on cabinets and trim.
Test the same color in two sheens on poster board first, because sheen changes how the color looks in your light.
body:
Use flat for ceilings, eggshell for most living room and bedroom walls, satin for kitchens, baths, and kids rooms, and semi-gloss for trim, doors, and cabinets. Sheen is how much light the dry paint reflects, and as sheen goes up, washability goes up and wall flaws show more.

## The four finishes in one table

Sherwin-Williams and Behr sell the same ladder of sheens, with small name changes. Behr lists Flat, Matte, Eggshell Enamel, Satin Enamel, Semi-Gloss Enamel, and Hi-Gloss Enamel. The room advice lines up across both makers.

| Finish | Shine | Washability | Hides flaws | Best use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Flat | None | Low | Best | Ceilings, low traffic walls |
| Eggshell | Low, soft | Medium | Good | Living rooms, dining rooms, bedrooms |
| Satin | Medium, pearl-like | High | Fair | Kitchens, baths, halls, kids rooms |
| Semi-gloss | High, sleek | Very high | Poor | Trim, doors, cabinets, high moisture areas |

Behr describes flat as a low sheen, non-reflective finish that touches up well and hides minor flaws, made for low traffic areas, walls, and ceilings. Eggshell has a soft, velvety look for moderate traffic areas such as living rooms. Satin has a soft pearl-like look for moderate to high traffic areas and rooms with moisture, such as kitchens and baths. Semi-gloss has a sleek, radiant look for cabinets and trim, high traffic areas, and high moisture areas.

Sherwin-Williams makes the same point in its gloss and sheen guide: gloss and sheen change how you see color, and a matte color can look darker from an angle or in low light, while a glossy color can look lighter or show a rough surface. That is why the same can of color can look like two colors on a wall and on trim.

One step above semi-gloss sits high-gloss. It is the most durable and least forgiving. Save it for a front door or furniture. On a normal wall it shows every patch and roller line.

## Worked example: picking finishes for a 12 x 12 ft bedroom

Say you are painting a 12 x 12 ft (3.7 x 3.7 m) bedroom with 8 ft ceilings, one door, a small closet door, and trim round the room. You want one color on the walls, white on the ceiling and trim.

Ceiling pick: flat white. The ceiling gets little touch, flat hides tape joints and small waves in the drywall, and flat touches up with no visible lap lines. If the ceiling has water stains, prime them first or they will show through flat paint.

Wall pick: eggshell in your color. A bedroom is moderate traffic. Eggshell wipes clean with a damp cloth for small marks, still hides minor flaws, and does not shine under a bedside lamp. If kids or pets will rub the walls daily, step up to satin on the walls and accept that patches will show a bit more.

Trim and door pick: semi-gloss white. Baseboards, door frames, and doors take kicks, vacuum bumps, and hand marks. Semi-gloss scrubs clean and its shine sets the trim apart from eggshell walls, even in the same white. Sand trim smooth and fill dents before you coat, because semi-gloss will point at every dent you leave.

Amount check. Wall area = (12 + 12 + 12 + 12) ft x 8 ft = 384 sq ft. Take off about 40 sq ft for doors and windows and you have about 344 sq ft. At one gallon per 350 to 400 sq ft per coat in maker guidance for smooth walls, one gallon per coat is close, so two coats need 2 gallons of eggshell, rounded up like a buyer. Run your own room in our [paint calculator](/blog/paint-calculator/) for an exact count, and read our guide on [how many coats of paint](/blog/how-many-coats-of-paint/) before you buy.

## How to pick by room and by wall condition

Start with use, then look at the wall. A kitchen, bath, entry, hall, and kids room get hands, steam, and food spots, so satin on walls is the safe default there. A living room, dining room, and adult bedroom get less wear, so eggshell gives a softer look with enough washability for most homes. Formal rooms with good walls can take flat or matte for a calm, low shine look, if you accept harder cleaning.

Wall condition can overrule the room rule. Old plaster with patches or drywall with a wavy joint will look worse in satin and far worse in semi-gloss. In that case, drop one sheen level and fix the worst flaws first. Test on the worst wall, not the best one.

Baths need care on the ceiling too. A flat ceiling in a small steamy bath can spot and mildew. Many painters use satin on bath ceilings and walls near the shower.

Outside, the same ladder holds. Flat and satin are common on siding, satin and semi-gloss on trim and doors.

## Common sheen mistakes and small pro tips

The most common mistake is semi-gloss on a full wall. It looks shiny, shows every flaw, and is hard to touch up. Save it for trim and doors. The next mistake is flat paint in a hall or kids room. It marks fast, and scrubbing can leave a shiny spot in the flat film.

Touch-ups blend best in flat and worst in higher sheens. For a wall that gets touched up a lot, eggshell is a good middle pick. Keep a small sealed jar of the exact paint and sheen for each room, with the room name on the lid.

Buy sheen by surface, not by room alone. One room often needs three sheens: flat on the ceiling, eggshell or satin on walls, semi-gloss on trim. Cut in corners first, then roll while the edge is still wet, so sheen stays even. Behr advises multiple thin coats over one thick coat for semi-gloss and hi-gloss.

Primer changes sheen too. A patch primed with flat primer can flash through a satin top coat as a dull spot. Check our [primer calculator](/blog/primer-calculator/) for amounts. On new drywall, primer is not optional if you want an even sheen.

## Frequently asked questions

### What paint finish is best for living room walls?
Eggshell is the best default for most living rooms. Behr lists eggshell for moderate traffic areas such as living rooms, and it wipes clean better than flat while still hiding minor flaws.

### Is satin or eggshell better for a kitchen?
Satin is better for most kitchens. Behr lists satin for areas with moisture and higher traffic, such as kitchens and baths. It scrubs clean more easily than eggshell and holds up to steam and grease spots.

### What finish should trim and doors be?
Semi-gloss is the standard pick for trim, doors, and cabinets. Behr lists semi-gloss for cabinets and trim and for high traffic and high moisture areas. It is hard, washable, and makes trim stand out from the walls.

### Does sheen change the paint color?
Yes, in how it looks. Sherwin-Williams notes that dark glossy paint can look darker straight on, light glossy paint can look brighter, and matte paint can look darker from an angle or in low light. Test your color in the sheen you will use.

### Can I use flat paint in a bathroom?
You can in a large, well vented bath, but satin is safer in a small steamy bath. Flat is harder to clean and can spot with moisture. Use the fan, and pick satin on walls near the tub or shower.

### What is the difference between matte and flat?
Both are low shine. Behr lists matte as a low luster finish that is durable, easy to clean, and touches up well, while flat is the lowest sheen and best at hiding flaws. In many lines, matte is a step more washable than flat.
